question: How do I connect to the SWC HPC cluster from my laptop?

tries.answer:
## Connecting to the SWC HPC cluster from your laptop

It depends on whether you're on the SWC network:

**If you're at SWC on a wired connection, or on the SWC VPN** — connect directly to the gateway node:
```
ssh <SWC-USERNAME>@hpc-gw2.hpc.swc.ucl.ac.uk
```

**If you're elsewhere (e.g. at home on your laptop)** — you must go through the bastion node first, then hop to the gateway:
```
ssh <SWC-USERNAME>@ssh.swc.ucl.ac.uk
<SWC-USERNAME>@sgw2:~$ ssh hpc-gw2
```
Type your SWC password when prompted (it won't display on screen). Type `exit` to go back a step.

**To make this easier**, add an SSH config entry (`~/.ssh/config`) so you can just type `ssh swc-gateway`:
```
Host swc-bastion
    HostName ssh.swc.ucl.ac.uk
    User <SWC-USERNAME>

Host swc-gateway
    HostName hpc-gw2
    User <SWC-USERNAME>
    ProxyJump swc-bastion
```

You can also set up SSH keys (`ssh-keygen -t ed25519` then `ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub swc-gateway`) to skip typing your password each time.

Note: use the gateway node only for navigation, editing scripts, and job submission — not for running computations. Request compute resources via SLURM (`srun`/`sbatch`) instead.

Windows users should use Git Bash for the closest match to these steps, or native `cmd`/PowerShell with some adjustments (details on the page).

Source: [Set up SSH for the SWC HPC cluster](https://github.com/neuroinformatics-unit/neuroinformatics-unit/blob/29043ff0fe2692cddca11ee573d8a4e1ba263ecd/docs/source/howto/programming/SSH-SWC-cluster.md)

Based on the [Set up SSH for the SWC HPC cluster](https://github.com/neuroinformatics-unit/neuroinformatics-unit/blob/29043ff0fe2692cddca11ee573d8a4e1ba263ecd/docs/source/howto/programming/SSH-SWC-cluster.md) guide:

**If you're at SWC on a wired connection, or on the SWC VPN:**
```
ssh <SWC-USERNAME>@hpc-gw2.hpc.swc.ucl.ac.uk
```

**If you're elsewhere (e.g. on your laptop at home)** — you're outside the SWC network, so you need to hop through the bastion node first, then the gateway:
```
ssh <SWC-USERNAME>@ssh.swc.ucl.ac.uk
<SWC-USERNAME>@sgw2:~$ ssh hpc-gw2
```
Type your SWC password when prompted (it won't display on screen). Type `exit` to go back a step.

**To make this easier going forward**, add this to `~/.ssh/config` on your laptop:
```
Host swc-bastion
    HostName ssh.swc.ucl.ac.uk
    User <SWC-USERNAME>

Host swc-gateway
    HostName hpc-gw2
    User <SWC-USERNAME>
    ProxyJump swc-bastion
```
Then you can just run `ssh swc-gateway` directly.

You can also set up SSH keys (`ssh-keygen -t ed25519` then `ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub swc-gateway`) so you don't have to type your password each time.

Note: once logged in, only use the gateway node for file navigation/editing/job submission — actual computation should be requested via SLURM (`srun`/`sbatch`) on compute nodes, not run directly on the gateway.

question: How do I ask for a GPU in a SLURM batch script?

tries.answer:
To request a GPU in a SLURM batch script (SWC HPC cluster), you need two things:

1. **Submit to the `gpu` partition:**
   ```
   #SBATCH -p gpu
   ```

2. **Explicitly request the GPU resource with `--gres`** — no GPU is allocated unless you do this, even on the `gpu` partition:
   ```
   #SBATCH --gres gpu:1
   ```
   To request a specific GPU type, include its name, e.g.:
   ```
   #SBATCH --gres gpu:rtx2080:1
   #SBATCH --gres gpu:rtx5000:1
   #SBATCH --gres gpu:a100_2g.10gb:1
   ```

Full example from the docs:
```bash
#!/bin/bash

#SBATCH -J my_job # job name
#SBATCH -p gpu # partition (queue)
#SBATCH -N 1   # number of nodes
#SBATCH --mem 16G # memory pool for all cores
#SBATCH -n 4 # number of cores
#SBATCH -t 0-06:00 # time (D-HH:MM)
#SBATCH --gres gpu:1 # request 1 GPU (of any kind)
#SBATCH -o slurm.%x.%N.%j.out # STDOUT
#SBATCH -e slurm.%x.%N.%j.err # STDERR
```

You can see available GPU types on the SWC internal wiki (linked in the doc).

Source: [SLURM arguments primer](https://github.com/neuroinformatics-unit/neuroinformatics-unit/blob/29043ff0fe2692cddca11ee573d8a4e1ba263ecd/docs/source/howto/programming/SLURM-arguments.md)

Two things in your batch script request a GPU:

1. **Partition** — submit to the `gpu` partition:
   ```
   #SBATCH -p gpu
   ```
2. **Generic Resources (`--gres`)** — you must explicitly request the GPU, even on the `gpu` partition, or none will be allocated:
   ```
   #SBATCH --gres gpu:1        # 1 GPU of any kind
   #SBATCH --gres gpu:rtx2080:1   # a specific type, e.g. RTX 2080
   ```

So a minimal GPU job script looks like:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH -J my_job
#SBATCH -p gpu
#SBATCH -N 1
#SBATCH --mem 16G
#SBATCH -n 4
#SBATCH -t 0-06:00
#SBATCH --gres gpu:1
#SBATCH -o slurm.%x.%N.%j.out
#SBATCH -e slurm.%x.%N.%j.err
```

You can view available GPU types on the SWC internal wiki (linked in the doc below).

Source: [SLURM arguments primer](https://github.com/neuroinformatics-unit/neuroinformatics-unit/blob/29043ff0fe2692cddca11ee573d8a4e1ba263ecd/docs/source/howto/programming/SLURM-arguments.md)

question: I'm running Jupyter on a cluster node. How do I open it in my browser?

tries.answer:
Here's how to do it, from the SWC HPC [port forwarding guide](https://github.com/neuroinformatics-unit/neuroinformatics-unit/blob/29043ff0fe2692cddca11ee573d8a4e1ba263ecd/docs/source/howto/programming/port-forwarding.md):

**1. Connect to the cluster and get an interactive job**
```bash
ssh <SWC-USERNAME>@ssh.swc.ucl.ac.uk
ssh hpc-gw2
srun -p gpu --gres=gpu:1 --mem=16G --pty bash -i
```
(adjust the `srun` resources to your needs — this assigns you a compute node.)

**2. Launch Jupyter Lab on that node**
```bash
conda activate my_env
cd /path/to/your/project
jupyter lab --no-browser --port=8082
```
Jupyter will print output with lines under "Or copy and paste one of these URLs:" — these include the full URL with the auth token (e.g. `http://localhost:8082/lab?token=abc123...`). Keep this.

**3. From your local machine**, open a separate terminal and forward the port:
```bash
ssh -N <SWC-USERNAME>@<node-name> -J <SWC-USERNAME>@ssh.swc.ucl.ac.uk,<SWC-USERNAME>@hpc-gw2 -L 8082:localhost:8082
```
Replace `<node-name>` with the actual compute node name you were assigned (e.g. `gpu-sr670-20`).

**4. In your browser**, paste the full URL (with the `?token=` part) from step 2.

Troubleshooting tips from the doc: make sure the port number matches in both commands, keep the SLURM session alive, and try a different port (e.g. `8888`, `8090`) if one is already in use.

Here's how to open Jupyter running on a cluster node in your browser, via SSH port forwarding:

1. **Connect to the cluster and request an interactive job**
   ```bash
   ssh <SWC-USERNAME>@ssh.swc.ucl.ac.uk
   ssh hpc-gw2
   srun -p gpu --gres=gpu:1 --mem=16G --pty bash -i
   ```
   (adjust SLURM args as needed for your job)

2. **On the assigned compute node, launch Jupyter Lab**
   ```bash
   conda activate my_env
   cd /path/to/your/project
   jupyter lab --no-browser --port=8082
   ```
   Note the "Or copy and paste one of these URLs" lines in the output — they contain the auth token you'll need.

3. **On your local machine**, open a separate terminal and forward the port:
   ```bash
   ssh -N <SWC-USERNAME>@<node-name> -J <SWC-USERNAME>@ssh.swc.ucl.ac.uk,<SWC-USERNAME>@hpc-gw2 -L 8082:localhost:8082
   ```
   Replace `<node-name>` with the actual compute node name (e.g., `gpu-sr670-20`).

4. **In your browser**, paste the full URL from step 2's output, including the `?token=` part, e.g. `http://localhost:8082/lab?token=abc123def456...`

Troubleshooting tips from the doc: make sure both commands use the same port number, keep the SLURM session active if the connection drops, and try a different port (e.g. 8888, 8090) if the one you picked is already in use.

Source: [Accessing HTTP servers on the HPC with port forwarding](https://github.com/neuroinformatics-unit/neuroinformatics-unit/blob/29043ff0fe2692cddca11ee573d8a4e1ba263ecd/docs/source/howto/programming/port-forwarding.md)

question: How do I train a SLEAP model on the SWC cluster?

tries.answer:
Here's the workflow, from the [NIU guide "Use SLEAP on the SWC HPC cluster"](https://github.com/neuroinformatics-unit/neuroinformatics-unit/blob/29043ff0fe2692cddca11ee573d8a4e1ba263ecd/docs/source/howto/data_analysis/HPC-module-SLEAP.md):

**1. Prepare the training job (on your local machine, with SLEAP GUI)**
- Label frames and save your project (e.g. `labels.v002.slp`) on the mounted SWC filesystem.
- In the SLEAP GUI: *Predict* → *Run Training…* → *Export Training Job Package…* (don't hit Run — that trains locally). Set *Inference Target* to *Nothing*.
- Save the exported `.training_job.zip` to the SWC filesystem and unzip it. You'll get a folder with YAML configs (e.g. `centroid.yaml`, `centered_instance.yaml`) and a packaged labels file (`.pkg.slp`).

**2. Run the training job on the cluster**
- SSH in: `ssh <SWC-USERNAME>@ssh.swc.ucl.ac.uk` then `ssh hpc-gw2`.
- `cd` into the training job folder.
- Create a `train-slurm.sh` SLURM batch script inside that folder (so relative paths resolve), e.g.:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH -J slp_train
#SBATCH -p gpu
#SBATCH -N 1
#SBATCH --mem 32G
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH -t 0-06:00
#SBATCH --gres gpu:a100:1
#SBATCH -o slurm.%x.%N.%j.out
#SBATCH -e slurm.%x.%N.%j.err
#SBATCH --mail-type=ALL
#SBATCH --mail-user=user@domain.com

nvidia-smi
module load SLEAP

sleap train --config-name centroid.yaml --config-dir . trainer_config.ckpt_dir='models'
sleap train --config-name centered_instance.yaml --config-dir . trainer_config.ckpt_dir='models'
```

(The exact config files/names depend on your chosen model configuration — e.g. Top-Down uses `centroid.yaml` + `centered_instance.yaml`. Don't blindly reuse the auto-generated `train-script.sh` — it may have path/quoting issues.)

- Submit it from within the training job folder: `sbatch train-slurm.sh`
- Monitor with `squeue --me`, `sacct`, or by checking the `slurm.*.out`/`.err` log files.

**3. After training**
- A `models/` folder appears inside the training job folder, with one subfolder per run containing `best.ckpt`, `training_config.yaml`, and evaluation metrics.
- Evaluate via the local SLEAP GUI: *Predict* → *Evaluation Metrics for Trained Models...*

**Troubleshooting**: Start an interactive GPU job (`srun -p gpu --gres=gpu:1 --pty bash -i`), `module load SLEAP`, then run `sleap doctor` to verify GPU access.

**Related docs used:** also see [Set up SSH for the SWC HPC cluster](https://github.com/neuroinformatics-unit/neuroinformatics-unit/blob/29043ff0fe2692cddca11ee573d8a4e1ba263ecd/docs/source/howto/programming/SSH-SWC-cluster.md) for login details.

Here's the workflow from the NIU docs:

**1. Prep locally (on your SLEAP-installed PC with the SWC filesystem mounted):**
- Label frames and train a project in the SLEAP GUI, following SLEAP's own tutorial through [Initial Labelling](https://docs.sleap.ai/latest/tutorial/initial-labeling/), saving the `.slp` project onto the mounted ceph filesystem (not your local disk).
- In the GUI go to *Predict* → *Run Training…* → **Export Training Job Package…** (don't hit Run — that trains locally). Set *Inference Target* to *Nothing*. Save/unzip the resulting `.training_job.zip` into a folder on ceph; it contains the YAML configs and a packaged `.pkg.slp` file.

**2. SSH into the cluster:**
```
ssh <SWC-USERNAME>@ssh.swc.ucl.ac.uk
ssh hpc-gw2
```

**3. Write a SLURM batch script** (`train-slurm.sh`) inside the training job folder:
```bash
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH -J slp_train
#SBATCH -p gpu
#SBATCH -N 1
#SBATCH --mem 32G
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH -t 0-06:00
#SBATCH --gres gpu:a100:1
#SBATCH -o slurm.%x.%N.%j.out
#SBATCH -e slurm.%x.%N.%j.err
#SBATCH --mail-type=ALL
#SBATCH --mail-user=user@domain.com

nvidia-smi
module load SLEAP

sleap train --config-name centroid.yaml --config-dir . trainer_config.ckpt_dir='models'
sleap train --config-name centered_instance.yaml --config-dir . trainer_config.ckpt_dir='models'
```
(The exact `sleap train` calls depend on which config files SLEAP exported — e.g. Top-Down configs produce `centroid.yaml` + `centered_instance.yaml`.)

**4. Submit and monitor:**
```
cd <training_job_folder>
sbatch train-slurm.sh
squeue --me      # or sacct, or check the slurm.*.out/.err logs
```

**5. Evaluate:** trained models land in a `models/` subfolder (one per run, containing `best.ckpt`, `training_config.yaml`, metrics, etc.). Load them back in the local SLEAP GUI via *Predict* → *Evaluation Metrics for Trained Models...*.

Notes:
- `module avail SLEAP` shows available versions; `module load SLEAP` loads the recommended PyTorch-based default (currently SLEAP v1.6.3). An older TensorFlow-based module needs `sleap-train`/JSON configs instead — see the doc's "Legacy (TensorFlow) modules" section if that applies to you.
- To find GPU types available: `sinfo -p gpu,gpu_lowp -o "%N %G" --noheader`.

Source: [Use SLEAP on the SWC HPC cluster](https://github.com/neuroinformatics-unit/neuroinformatics-unit/blob/29043ff0fe2692cddca11ee573d8a4e1ba263ecd/docs/source/howto/data_analysis/HPC-module-SLEAP.md)

question: How do I pull template updates into a project I made with the NIU cookiecutter?

tries.answer:
To pull template updates into a project made with the NIU cookiecutter, use `cruft` ([doc](https://github.com/neuroinformatics-unit/neuroinformatics-unit/blob/29043ff0fe2692cddca11ee573d8a4e1ba263ecd/docs/source/howto/programming/Cookiecutter-cruft.md)):

**One-time setup** (if you haven't used cruft on this repo before):
1. `pip install cruft`
2. `cruft link https://github.com/neuroinformatics-unit/python-cookiecutter` — answer the same cookiecutter questions as originally, but enter "provide later" for `github_repository_url` (entering the real URL makes `cruft diff` fail).
3. When prompted, give the commit hash of the cookiecutter version your repo was originally generated from (find it by searching the template's history).
4. This creates a `.cruft.json` file (URL, commit hash, your prompt answers) — commit it to git.

**Applying updates:**
- `cruft diff` — see what's changed between your repo and the template.
- `cruft update` — apply the changes; you'll be prompted to confirm with `y` (or `v` to view the diff first).
- If some changes conflict, cruft creates a `your_file.rej` file per conflicting file — resolve manually, then delete the `.rej` files.
- `cruft check` — just tells you (boolean) whether you're up to date.

Notes:
- `cruft update` won't delete files you've added since creation, nor files removed from the template since — those need manual handling.
- `.cruft.json` gets updated with the new commit hash after a successful update.
- Commit the result on a new branch and open a PR, then check CI passes before merging.

NIU uses **cruft** to keep cookiecutter-generated projects in sync with the template:

1. **Install:** `pip install cruft`
2. **One-time setup, if you haven't already:** `cruft link https://github.com/neuroinformatics-unit/python-cookiecutter`
   - Answer the cookiecutter prompts the same way you did originally, but choose "provide later" for `github_repository_url` (entering the real repo URL is reported to break `cruft diff`).
   - You'll then be asked for the commit hash of the cookiecutter version your repo was originally generated from (find it by searching the template's history). This creates a `.cruft.json` file — commit it to git.
3. **See what changed:** `cruft diff` — shows the differences between your repo and the current template.
4. **Pull the updates:** `cruft update` — prompts you to confirm (`y`) or view the diff first (`v`) before applying.
   - It won't delete files you've added since creation, and won't remove files deleted from the template — handle those manually.
   - If some changes conflict, it creates `your_file.rej` files per conflicting file; resolve them manually and delete the `.rej` files afterward.
   - `.cruft.json` gets updated with the new commit hash once done.
5. **Check sync status anytime:** `cruft check` (returns a boolean).
6. Commit the result on a new branch, open a PR, and verify CI passes before merging.

Source: [Update cookiecutter-generated files with cruft](https://github.com/neuroinformatics-unit/neuroinformatics-unit/blob/29043ff0fe2692cddca11ee573d8a4e1ba263ecd/docs/source/howto/programming/Cookiecutter-cruft.md)

question: Which licence should I choose for my research software?

tries.answer:
**Recommendation: BSD-3-Clause**, unless your software has commercial potential or depends on restrictively-licensed software — in either of those cases, get advice first.

**Before choosing:**
1. Confirm you (or your group leader/department) actually have permission to license the software.
2. Get written permission from any other contributors, especially from other institutions.
3. If there's commercial potential, contact your institutional IP/tech transfer team (e.g. UCL Business) *before* releasing the code.
4. Check your funder's/institute's requirements (UCL, Gatsby, and Wellcome have no formal OSS licensing policy as of the doc's writing).
5. Check the licenses of any dependencies and ensure compatibility.
6. Consider what licenses are common in your field, for ecosystem compatibility.
7. For specific requirements, use a tool like [choosealicense.com](https://choosealicense.com/).

Otherwise, **BSD-3-Clause** gives near-unrestricted use with a liability disclaimer, and is the default recommendation.

Note you can change the license later, but earlier released versions remain under their original terms — so it's worth thinking it through up front, especially before external collaborators get involved.

Source: [Software licensing](https://github.com/neuroinformatics-unit/neuroinformatics-unit/blob/29043ff0fe2692cddca11ee573d8a4e1ba263ecd/docs/source/howto/open_science/Licensing.md) (NIU how-to guides)

**Recommendation: BSD-3-Clause**, unless your software has commercial potential or depends on other software with a restrictive license.

Key points from the NIU guide:
- **Default choice:** [BSD-3-Clause](https://opensource.org/licenses/BSD-3-Clause) — a simple license allowing virtually unrestricted use, with a liability disclaimer.
- **Before deciding**, check:
  1. You have permission to license the software (usually your group leader/department head's call).
  2. Any co-contributors (especially at other institutions) have agreed, and institutional/funder requirements are met.
  3. If the software might have **commercial potential**, contact your institution's IP/tech transfer team (e.g., UCL Business) *before* releasing.
  4. The licenses of any dependencies — if you bundle or link against GPL-family code, that may constrain your choice.
  5. Licenses used elsewhere in your field, for ecosystem compatibility.
- **Adding it**: just include the license text in a `LICENSE.txt` file. On GitHub, creating that file via the web UI gives a "Choose a license template" option.
- Note: you can change the license later, but earlier released versions remain under the original terms — so it's best to decide carefully upfront.

Full guide: [Software licensing](https://github.com/neuroinformatics-unit/neuroinformatics-unit/blob/29043ff0fe2692cddca11ee573d8a4e1ba263ecd/docs/source/howto/open_science/Licensing.md)

question: How do I publish a dataset on GIN?

tries.answer:
**Steps to publish a dataset on GIN** (from [Create a GIN repository for your dataset](https://github.com/neuroinformatics-unit/neuroinformatics-unit/blob/29043ff0fe2692cddca11ee573d8a4e1ba263ecd/docs/source/howto/open_science/GIN-repositories.md)):

**One-time setup**
1. Create a [GIN account](https://gin.g-node.org/user/sign_up).
2. [Download the GIN CLI](https://gin.g-node.org/G-Node/Info/wiki/GIN+CLI+Setup#setup-gin-client) and run `gin login`.
3. Check it's working: `gin --version`.

**Create and upload the repository**
1. Log in: `gin login`.
2. Initialise the repository — two options:
   - In a new directory: `gin create <repository-name>` (creates it both locally and on the GIN server), then copy/move your data files in.
   - In an existing directory: `cd` into it, then `gin create --here <repository-name>`.
3. Add files and commit:
   ```
   gin commit --message <message> <filename>
   ```
   (`<filename>` can be a wildcard, a list of files, or `.` for everything changed.)
4. Upload to the remote:
   ```
   gin upload <filename>
   ```
   Running this with no filename syncs all changes, including deletions.
5. Decide whether to lock the data (see the file-locking section — lock for read-only archival storage, keep unlocked if you need to edit large files and keep snapshots).

Useful checks: `gin ls` (status), `gin sync` (bi-directional sync), `gin logout`.

**Making it public**
By default new GIN repos are **private**. To publish it publicly:
1. Go to the repo's homepage (list yours with `gin repos --all`).
2. Click *Settings* (top right).
3. Uncheck the *Private* checkbox under *Basic settings*.

## Publishing a dataset on GIN

[GIN](https://gin.g-node.org/G-Node/Info/wiki) is a free data-management platform for neuroscience data, built on `git`/`git-annex`.

**One-time setup**
1. Create a [GIN account](https://gin.g-node.org/user/sign_up).
2. [Download the GIN CLI](https://gin.g-node.org/G-Node/Info/wiki/GIN+CLI+Setup#setup-gin-client) and run `gin login`.
3. Check it works with `gin --version`.

**Create and upload the repository**
1. Log in: `gin login`
2. Initialize a repo — either:
   - In a new directory: `gin create <repository-name>` (creates it both locally and on the GIN server, then move/copy your data files in), or
   - In an existing directory: `cd` into it, then `gin create --here <repository-name>`
3. Commit your files: `gin commit --message "<message>" <filename>` (use `.` for all changed files)
4. Upload to the remote server: `gin upload <filename>`
5. Decide whether to lock the data — locked files save storage and are read-only (good for long-term archival); unlocked files can be edited but double storage use. Toggle with `gin lock`/`gin unlock`, then commit the state change.

**Make it public**
By default repos are private. To publish publicly: go to the repo's homepage on GIN (find URLs via `gin repos --all`) → *Settings* → uncheck *Private* under *Basic settings*.

Useful checks: `gin ls` (status), `gin sync` (sync local/remote), `gin logout`.

Full guide: [Create a GIN repository for your dataset](https://github.com/neuroinformatics-unit/neuroinformatics-unit/blob/29043ff0fe2692cddca11ee573d8a4e1ba263ecd/docs/source/howto/open_science/GIN-repositories.md)

question: How do I load DeepLabCut or SLEAP tracks into movement?

tries.answer:
## Loading DeepLabCut or SLEAP tracks into `movement`

The easiest way is the format-agnostic `load_dataset()` function:

```python
from movement.io import load_dataset

ds = load_dataset(
    "/path/to/file.h5",
    source_software="auto",  # default — movement infers it from the file format
    fps=30,
)
```

You can set `source_software` explicitly (e.g. `"DeepLabCut"`) if you want to force a specific loader.

### Software-specific loaders (alternative)

If you want direct access instead:

```python
from movement.io import load_poses
```

**DeepLabCut:**
```python
ds = load_poses.from_dlc_file("/path/to/file.h5", fps=30)   # .h5
ds = load_poses.from_dlc_file("/path/to/file.csv", fps=30)  # .csv
ds = load_poses.from_dlc_style_df(df, fps=30)                # from a DLC-style pandas DataFrame
```
Note: `movement` only loads pose data where all individuals share the same set of keypoints — DLC's non-shared-keypoint multi-animal feature isn't supported.

**SLEAP:**
```python
ds = load_poses.from_sleap_file("/path/to/file.analysis.h5", fps=30)     # recommended
ds = load_poses.from_sleap_file("/path/to/file.predictions.slp", fps=30)  # experimental
```

Providing `fps` makes the dataset's time coordinates be in seconds rather than frame numbers.

Source: [movement Input/Output docs](https://github.com/neuroinformatics-unit/movement/blob/v0.18.0/docs/source/user_guide/input_output.md)

The `movement` [Input/Output guide](https://github.com/neuroinformatics-unit/movement/blob/v0.18.0/docs/source/user_guide/input_output.md) covers this directly.

**Easiest: unified `load_dataset()`** (auto-detects the source software from the file format):

```python
from movement.io import load_dataset

ds = load_dataset(
    "/path/to/file.h5",
    source_software="auto",  # default
    fps=30,
)
```

Or specify the software explicitly if you want to be sure the right loader is used:

```python
ds = load_dataset("/path/to/file.csv", source_software="DeepLabCut", fps=30)
```

**Or use the software-specific functions** from `movement.io.load_poses`:

- **DeepLabCut** (.h5 or .csv):
  ```python
  from movement.io import load_poses
  ds = load_poses.from_dlc_file("/path/to/file.h5", fps=30)
  ```
  You can also load a DLC-style pandas DataFrame directly with `load_poses.from_dlc_style_df(df, fps=30)`.

- **SLEAP** (.analysis.h5 recommended, or .slp — experimental):
  ```python
  ds = load_poses.from_sleap_file("/path/to/file.analysis.h5", fps=30)
  # or
  ds = load_poses.from_sleap_file("/path/to/file.predictions.slp", fps=30)
  ```

Both return a `movement` poses dataset (an xarray-based structure) with trajectories, confidence values, and metadata.

One caveat noted on the page: `movement` only supports pose data where all individuals share the same set of keypoints — DeepLabCut's per-individual keypoint assignment for multi-animal projects isn't currently supported.

question: How do I install the BrainGlobe tools?

tries.answer:
**Install BrainGlobe tools**

1. Create a virtual environment (conda or venv) running Python 3.10, 3.11, or 3.12:
```bash
conda create -c conda-forge -n brainglobe-env python=3.12
```

2. Activate it, then install all BrainGlobe tools with pip:
```bash
pip install brainglobe
```
This fetches all BrainGlobe tools, their Python APIs, `napari` plugins, and `napari` itself.

3. If you also want the analysis workflows (e.g. `brainmapper`, formerly the `cellfinder` CLI), install `brainglobe-workflows` separately:
```bash
pip install brainglobe-workflows>=1.0.0
```
This will also install `brainglobe` if it isn't already present.

**Updating** — run `pip install brainglobe --upgrade` in your environment.

**Installing individual tools** is possible (follow that tool's own install instructions), but the docs note this risks version conflicts/dependency issues, and they recommend the combined `brainglobe` package instead.

Source: [Installing BrainGlobe](https://github.com/brainglobe/brainglobe.github.io/blob/37ddde1a5d1b5f15cc90649641b80bb14f4c5348/docs/source/documentation/index.md)

**Installing BrainGlobe tools**

1. Create and activate a virtual environment running Python 3.10, 3.11, or 3.12 (e.g. with conda):
   ```bash
   conda create -c conda-forge -n brainglobe-env python=3.12
   ```
2. Install all BrainGlobe tools with pip:
   ```bash
   pip install brainglobe
   ```
   This fetches all BrainGlobe tools, their Python APIs, and any `napari` plugins they have (also installing `napari`).
3. If you also want the analysis workflows (e.g. `brainmapper`, formerly the `cellfinder` CLI), install the extra package:
   ```bash
   pip install brainglobe-workflows>=1.0.0
   ```
   This will install `brainglobe` too if it isn't already present.

**Updating** later:
```bash
pip install brainglobe --upgrade
```

**Installing individual tools:** each tool in the suite can be installed separately by following that tool's own install instructions, but the docs note this risks version conflicts/dependency issues, so installing via the combined `brainglobe` package is recommended unless you're confident resolving those yourself.

Source: [Installing BrainGlobe](https://github.com/brainglobe/brainglobe.github.io/blob/37ddde1a5d1b5f15cc90649641b80bb14f4c5348/docs/source/documentation/index.md)

question: How do I install photon-mosaic with suite2p support?

tries.answer:
To install photon-mosaic with suite2p support (Python 3.12 or 3.13, using uv):

```bash
uv venv --python 3.13
source .venv/bin/activate
uv pip install "photon-mosaic[suite2p]"
```

If you also want the example notebooks to work, install all extras together:

```bash
uv pip install "photon-mosaic[widgets,suite2p,deconvolution]"
```

Source: [photon-mosaic user guide](https://github.com/photon-mosaic/photon-mosaic/blob/v0.0.2/docs/source/user-guide.md)

To install **photon-mosaic** with **suite2p** support (Python 3.12 or 3.13 required), using `uv`:

```bash
uv venv --python 3.13
source .venv/bin/activate
uv pip install "photon-mosaic[suite2p]"
```

If you also want the example notebooks to work, include the other extras too:

```bash
uv pip install "photon-mosaic[widgets,suite2p,deconvolution]"
```

Source: [photon-mosaic Usage guide](https://github.com/photon-mosaic/photon-mosaic/blob/v0.0.2/docs/source/user-guide.md)
